summary: Defines a framework for applying security services to MIME body parts, with multipart/signed for digital signatures and multipart/encrypted for encryption. It is a standards-track document.

eli5.summary: Two kinds of special envelope for email: one has a signature to prove who wrote it, and one is locked.

subtitle: Two MIME wrappers that carry protected data and the control information needed to verify or unlock it.

tldr.problem: MIME describes the format of Internet mail bodies but provides no security protection of its own.
tldr.mechanism: It defines two multipart subtypes, signed and encrypted, each with exactly two body parts: the protected data and the control information. A required protocol parameter says what the control information is.
tldr.outcome: By itself the RFC specifies no security protection. It is a framework, and each security protocol must be defined in a separate document that plugs in through the protocol parameter.

today: RFC 1847 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The RFC itself defines only the framework, not any particular signing or encryption protocol.

sections.title: Why MIME Needs a Security Framework
sections.content:
An Internet mail message has headers and a body. The headers follow RFC 822, and a structured body follows MIME (RFC 1521). The basic MIME specification does not provide specific security protection.

This RFC defines a framework so that security services supplied by other protocols can be used with MIME. By itself it does not specify security protection. A MIME agent needs support for both this framework and a mechanism to interact with a security protocol defined in a separate document.
sections.eli5: MIME is like a mailroom that knows how to pack parcels but has no locks. This RFC adds a standard way to attach locks that other people design.

sections.title: Two Security Subtypes of Multipart
sections.content:
The framework adds two new subtypes of the MIME multipart content type: signed and encrypted. In each, there are exactly two related body parts: one for the protected data and one for the control information.

The multipart/signed type supports authentication and integrity through a digital signature, and its control information is in the second part. The multipart/encrypted type supports confidentiality through encryption, and its control information is in the first part.

Both types require a protocol parameter. Its value decides the type and contents of the control information part. New protocols are added by registering new values for it. A MIME agent that does not recognize the value cannot process the security multipart, but it may still process any other body parts present.
sections.eli5: Each envelope has exactly two compartments: one for the message and one for the instructions. A label on the outside says which kind of instructions are inside.

sections.title: The Multipart/Signed Format
sections.content:
A multipart/signed object has the required parameters boundary, protocol and micalg, and no optional ones. The first body part is the part over which the signature was made, including its MIME headers, and it may be any valid MIME type. The second part holds the control information needed to verify the signature, labeled by the protocol value.

The micalg parameter names the algorithm for the Message Integrity Check (MIC), the quantity computed over the body part with a message digest or hash function. Its value may be a comma-separated list when multiple algorithms are used. If the control information also names the algorithm and the two disagree, that is an error. The parameter exists to support one-pass processing: an implementation can compute the MIC while reading the first part until it reaches the boundary of the second.

The whole container must be treated as opaque in transit. Intermediate message transfer agents must not alter it, including changing the content transfer encoding of any part. The signature covers only material inside the object, not enclosing message material or entities referenced rather than included.

If a signed object may ever cross standard Internet SMTP, its body is constrained to 7 bits. Any 8bit or binary material MUST be encoded as quoted-printable or base64, because converting it later would invalidate the signature.
sections.eli5: A signed message is a letter with a seal-note stapled behind it. Nobody along the way may rewrite the letter, or the seal would no longer match.

sections.title: Signing and Verifying Steps
sections.content:
The RFC describes a three-step process for each direction. It stresses that the steps are descriptive, not prescriptive.

To create a signed part: prepare the content as a MIME body part in canonical format with its headers; prepare it for signature according to the protocol value, including the MIME headers so the labeling is protected; then hand it to the signature process, which returns the control information (placed in the second part) and the signed body part (the first part).

To verify: prepare the first part and the control information per the protocol value, pass them to the verification process, and give the user the result. The MIME agent then continues with the body part that verification returned. Usually that is identical to the received part, but the RFC allows protocols that modify it.
sections.eli5: To sign, you pack the letter and get a seal-note. To check, you compare the letter with the seal-note and tell the reader whether they match.

sections.title: The Multipart/Encrypted Format
sections.content:
A multipart/encrypted object has the required parameters boundary and protocol, and no optional ones. The first body part holds the control information needed to decrypt, labeled by the protocol value. The second part holds the encrypted data and is always labeled application/octet-stream.

The MIME headers of the original body part are included in the encryption, so the labeling of the data is hidden too. As a result, the octet-stream data is itself a nested MIME body part. A receiver cannot display the second part as received, because the transformation is described in the control information rather than in the MIME headers. It should wait until the encryption is removed before trying to display anything.

The decryption result is likely to say whether it succeeded. Failure may come from a missing key or recipient field, and the data from a failed decryption is described as pretty much guaranteed to be garbage.
sections.eli5: An encrypted message is a key card in one compartment and a locked box in the other. You must unlock the box before you can see even what kind of thing is inside.

sections.title: Control Information and Key Management
sections.content:
A minimal MIME implementation can recognize both multipart types and identify the protected data and control information parts. Complete support means recognizing the protocol value and continuing based on it. That value is the same one used to label the content type of the control information.

The document that defines a security protocol must specify the protocol value, the processing it requires and the exact contents of the control information part.

That document must also account for distributing cryptographic material, for example a signer's public key. One possible approach is two extra body parts, one to request cryptographic information and one to return it, but a protocol may choose another mechanism.
sections.eli5: The envelope rules do not say how locks work. Whoever invents a lock must write down how it works and how to get its key.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC states that it describes an enhancement to MIME to support signed and encrypted body parts, so in that context the entire document is about security. The type registration for multipart/signed adds that it must be treated as opaque while in transit; the registration for multipart/encrypted lists no security considerations.
sections.eli5: The whole point of this RFC is safety, and the one big rule is: do not open and change a signed envelope while it travels.

data.title: A multipart/signed body part
data.code:
Content-Type: multipart/signed; protocol="TYPE/STYPE";
        micalg="MICALG"; boundary="Signed Boundary"

--Signed Boundary
Content-Type: text/plain; charset="us-ascii"

This is some text to be signed although it could be
any type of data, labeled accordingly, of course.

--Signed Boundary
Content-Type: TYPE/STYPE

CONTROL INFORMATION for protocol "TYPE/STYPE" would be here

--Signed Boundary--
